utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, document 1053, also paragraph 2.2. General, this is a document of the 16th of March, which again mentions dislocation of the Albanian population by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This confirms what has been said so far, but this refers to a part of the border towards Macedonia. And the reason given here is that NATO technical equipment will be brought into this area as part of the preparations for the forthcoming war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these documents exhaust the topic of KLA preparations for the offensive. In the next set of questions we will be dealing with terrorist activities, and we will begin with document 3D1033. This is a document dated the 19th of December, 1998. Could the witness please be shown paragraph 2.4. It's on page 2 of the B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a typical example of certain KLA activities which we have seen in these documents. What characterises this paragraph in your view?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of this paragraph go to show that the KLA in relation to all suspicious Albanians who they termed spies were subject to repressive measures, such as abduction and even liquidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Your Honours pay attention to the last paragraph on this document, that's 3.1, it's got nothing to do with this topic; but I'll take this opportunity to put this question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you will have before you now point 3.1 or paragraph 3.1 which refers --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it refers to Combat Group 1 of the 15th Armoured Brigade from Pristina, the security organs of the Pristina Corps are informing us that on the 19th of December this unit went to its training grounds in the area of Batlavsko Jezero for regular company exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, General, this document which is a report of the command of the Pristina Corps to the security section, it was not addressed to the General Staff, was it? If I understood you correctly, it was addressed to the security administration; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you said that the command of the Pristina Corps in the period up to the outbreak of war regularly briefed the security section?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Who reviewed these reports and how were they dealt with?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived, or rather, they were telegrams which arrived usually in the evening, and in the morning when we arrived at work they would all go to the chief of the security administration for him to read and he would extract the information he needed for the ongoing briefings. After that, I would read them as the assistant for counter-intelligence, and then they would be further dealt with by the operations and analytics people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the chief of the security administration at the time was General Aleksandar Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I wish to draw Their Honours attention to the fact that the definition of combat Group 1/15, combat Group of the 15th Armoured Brigade is also found in 3D1035 and 3D1052. General, did General Dimitrijevic in any way draw attention to or respond to at meetings of the security administration in connection with the reporting concerning this unit and the events in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if General Dimitrijevic suspected that his security organ was providing him with incorrect or imprecise information, what would his reaction have been?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have called on the telephone immediately and he would have referred to the telegram, he would have said what page and what paragraph it was in, and he would have demanded a more extensive report, he would have demanded clarification and further details.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And do you know, General, whether General Dimitrijevic ever responded or intervened in connection with this report that had to do with training exercises of the 15th or the company of the 15th Armoured Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't, because had he done so the more extensive report would have arrived and I would have seen it so I would know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the two exhibits I mentioned 3D1035 of the 24th of December, 1999 [as interpreted], and 3D1052 of the 5th of March, 1999 also describe the events in this area, and we will be referring to them in our analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, one more question. This refers to document 1038, paragraph 2.6. Let's go back again to the so-called spring offensive. This is a document of the 29th of December, 1998. Again, there is information mentioned here on KLA activities abroad. Could you tell Their Honours who Bardhyl Mahmuti?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bardhyl Mahmuti was a political representative of the separatist leadership abroad, and he belonged to the militant line headed by Adem Demaqi. He was very influential and had many contacts abroad, and among the Albanian political emigres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This document speaks for itself, it refers to the Podujevo area, and it envisages the sending of fresh terrorist groups into the area. This is the 29th of December, 1998. General, document 3D1040 also paragraph 2.6. It's possible that we have no English translation, but it's very brief. I will read this. "The State Security Service has at its disposal information" -- excuse me, it's 2.6. "On the 12th of January, 1999, in actions of the so-called KLA with the aim of intimidating the population of Kosovo and Metohija, two Albanians were killed in Urosevac and in Kosovska Mitrovica and two Serb women were expelled from the village of Obrandza in Podujevo municipality." General, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this confirms what has been said so far. It shows how they treated Albanians, honest, decent Albanians who did not wish to join in the armed violence, that they suffered the same fate as the Serbs. They had no mercy towards them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Document 1041, 3D1041, dated the 19th of January, 1999, paragraph 2.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no translation, so we'll ask the interpreters to assist once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The document says that: "Information available to the security -- State Security Service shows that on the 16th of January, 1999, in the house of Rrustem Kelmendi in the village of Bela Crkva, Orahovac municipality, a meeting of the staff of the so-called KLA was held, chaired by Ilir Popaj and attended by Durmi Gashi, Bajram Popaj, Zelfi Kelmendi, Hajrulah Kelmendi, and others and a decision was reached on carrying out terrorist actions against members of the MUP and the VJ on the Zrze-Orahovac road through the village of Bela Crkva with the aim of causing an armed incident which would be used as a pretext for an attack on the village and the taking of the village by members of the so-called KLA." General, this piece of information was obtained in an exchange with the State Security Service. In your testimony you explained that sometimes part of the information you obtained came through that source?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it happened very frequently in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will remind Their Honours of the testimony of a number of witnesses as to the events in the village of Bela Crkva, and when we have a translation of this document we will proceed to analyse it further. However in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can help us. Why would the KLA wish to attack Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely because there's a part of the text not read by Mr. Visnjic. They wanted to provoke a conflict with the MUP, take the village of Bela Crkva, and then move out the population and so on, and then say to the verification mission that the MUP had attacked Bela Crkva and expelled or killed the population and so on. It says here that after taking Bela Crkva they could massacre some Albanian civilians indiscriminately, and then they would try in a perfidious manner to bring in the verification mission and blame the MUP for what had happened. I don't know whether I've been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you aware of any Albanians who survived and can tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably yes, but I couldn't tell you right now. I think that could be checked if the Prosecution is interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Prosecution are very interested and they've led evidence about this. I'm interested on whether there might be some Defence evidence from people who say this is what actually happened rather than simply Serb intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to the best of our knowledge this event did not actually take place, but this was information which existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The action was being prepared, but why they gave up, that's a different question. The persons who attended the meeting are listed here, so all the elements are there to show that they were preparing this, but not all the actions they were preparing were actually carried out. There were probably some circumstances that prevented it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The event in the indictment happened considerably later, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's what I'm thinking. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Although there is some concern on the part of the Prosecution, perhaps it would be better just later, but I raise it now, that some of the matters discussed in these reports are matters that witnesses who testified would have been in a position to know about and comment about and was not put to these witnesses -- many of these witnesses when they testified. But I think we'll address that later and deliver our position on that point in more detail at a later time. But I think the rules provide clearly in respect to anything the Defence intends to rely upon that if the opportunity arises in cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses, they should have been given an opportunity to speak about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this an example?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm checking precisely what was asked of Bajram Popaj or one of the specific witnesses who is mentioned there -- and this is not the first time, so we are checking the records to see exactly what the witnesses were allowed to speak about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be allowed, perhaps I can just give you some information regarding these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This group of documents was obtained by General Ojdanic's Defence. I don't have this information right now in front of me, but less than two months ago -- not more than two months ago. And we had been trying to obtain it over the past three years, to say the least, in order to be able to verify some things. And another thing I want to note here is that I would be the luckiest person in the world to have had these documents when we had the witness from Bela Crkva, at least about whether the KLA was in that area or not and we did cross-examine on that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect it's because it's a complicated matter that Mr. Stamp is taking the approach he is, since we would find it difficult to resolve anything here and now. So you should continue. However, Mr. Visnjic, it's not particularly helpful to have snippets referred to from each document; on the other hand, we do understand that in relation to some of these you will wish to pin-point items on which the witness can supplement the material available in the document. But remember the position we've taken consistently here, that you have to prioritize. In the interests of everyone involved in the trial, including your co-accused in particular, you have to find ways of presenting a reasonable body of material within a reasonable time. And you don't have the luxury of going through absolutely every piece of material that in a different environment, in an ideal world, you might be able to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me just assure you that what we exhibited so far is not every single piece of the material, it's just the tip of the iceberg of the information contained in the documents that we exhibited in full through this witness. And in order to comply with your order in some way, the next topic I intend to deal, that is weapons supply, I just wanted to say to the Trial Chamber that 3D1044, items 2.7, 2.8; 3D1045, paragraph 3; and 3D1051, paragraph 2.4 speak about the arming and supplying the KLA. I don't want to waste our time. Please consider that I have examined the witness about those items, but I beg for your patience on the next topic. We will be using six documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, to be clear, though, Mr. Visnjic, I'm -- we're not making any order on this. We are simply trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Manage, as far as is possible, for us the way in which the case is presented. And if you were to disagree with any suggestion I made about the way in which you presented the evidence that would be your privilege and you would be able to present it, subject obviously to our overall control of the time taken in the interests of everyone. On the other hand, it's because -- it's complicated a little because you've adopted a different approach from the approach in the statement itself. The approach you've taken is very helpful. I think you were wise to change your approach. Here, though, we have a reference to a document 3D1044 -- two of them -- three of them, 44, 45, and 51. Now, are they actually referred to in the statement? It may be that they're not. Well, I've found 51. Now, you can take it if the witness refers in the statement to a document and there's no objection from any party to that document being exhibited to the extent that -- to being exhibited, then we will have regard to if it's referred to in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the documents are mentioned in paragraph 129 as a group of documents that includes those that I just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's bring this to a close slowly. Our last topic is the conduct of the members of the Kosovo Verification Mission and other foreign representatives in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija regarding the problems related to the KLA and the attack launched by NATO on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And in this respect I would like to tender our first document, 3D1030, paragraph 2.6. This is a document dated the 15th of December, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you will see paragraph 2.6 in front of you momentarily, but before it does -- well, it's already here. Can you please tell me how did the KLA understand the function of and how did it use the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they understood it to be- and they actually used the mission and abused it indeed or at least tried to abuse it- as party that was favourable to them, that favoured them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It says here that they considered the arrival of the mission to be favourable because they would be able to move freely and carry out their tasks. What tasks are they talking about, General, that the KLA carried out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could remember, this was the 15th of December. This is the time where -- when they were working on reorganizing and strengthening the KLA and taking all those actions aimed at the civilians, MUP, and the army, the time when they prepared for this long guerilla warfare that would start in March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, very much. The same document, paragraph 2.10.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That's in page 3 of the Serbian version, page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have English version on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is about a conversation that was intercepted by radio surveillance. Could you please tell us what it is all about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is it, radio surveillance?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's using equipment to listen in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.10.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, this is the 15th of December and this radio surveillance, listening in to the conversations, yielded information about two KLA members, they were talking to each other, and they said that it was a good thing that the verifiers were there because -- they say: "Now we are carry out our actions because the conditions are favourable now. They will not do anything to us."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like document 3D1041, paragraph 2.6. This is the document dated the 19th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General -- well, this document - and we don't have the translation so I will read it very briefly - "according to the State Security Service information, members of the OSCE verification mission on several occasions visited the area of the Vitina municipality, the village of Letnica, which is in the border belt facing Macedonia and the surrounding area, showing interest in specific buildings, facilities, the bridges, and locations for the helicopter landings." General, as far as you know, did the Kosovo Verification Mission need this information to control the cease-fire in force between the KLA and the security forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but I think that this was part of something else, preparations for what actually happened in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D1044, paragraph 2.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did happen in March in relation to these buildings, facilities, bridges, and locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Bonomy, this has to do with checking or determining possible locations for the helicopters, the strength of the bridges, because there were some indications as part of NATO actions that there could be a ground attack, that ground forces could be involved in the NATO interventions. And that is why the strength of the bridges is being checked and as for possible helicopter landing sites, of course we all know that forces come in and land using helicopters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, did the helicopters come in with troops and land on the areas inspected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, because there was no ground operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your intelligence was wrong, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not wrong. From the point of view of gathering information, analysing the terrain for a possible ground invasion. So on the basis of the information that was gathered, reports were sent in and that was being considered; but then it was decided that there would be no ground operation, only air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to name any people in the OSCE-KVM mission who were actively working in support of or in preparation for NATO action in March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I don't have any specific data because after all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you name any person you suspect from the KVM mission to have been operating under cover for NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, suspicion is one thing and data, verifiable data, accurate data, is another thing. As an intelligence officer I can express my suspicions, but I would not like to imply anything about anyone without having accurate, verified data. I do know that Mr. Walker was an intelligence officer and was quite favourable and that he probably did send intelligence reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps the answer to your question lies in document 3D1044, paragraph 1 -- paragraph 2.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I said that perhaps the answer to your question lies in document 3D1044, paragraph 2.1. I will read this document which says the following: "The available operative data from the security organise of the 14th kog indicate that some of the KDOM EU members, mostly members of the French armed forces, are being sent to the NATO rapid intervention force, stationed in the Republic of Macedonia. "One of them is Frederik Gauthier, who even before leaving Kosovo and Metohija stated that 'the use of NATO forces in early spring is certain,' and we bring this in connection with the announcements made by the terrorists of the so-called KLA, that in the same period they would carry out an incursion of the sabotage groups" -- or rather, I'm sorry, "that they would break through the state border of the Republic of Albania and start carrying out massive terrorist attacks against the VJ and the MUP in the whole territory of Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we now know that that didn't happen, which must be a factor to be taken account of in evaluating all of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we know that this did not happen, but we don't know that it was not being prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, the second part of this did happen, that in the same period they would cross the state border from the Republic of Albania and begin large-scale terrorist attacks. This did happen, and as you know from other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's a different matter. And I think this Chamber would also have to consider carefully the difference between KDOM and the KVM. My question was related to the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at the next exhibit, 3D1048. Your Honours, excuse me, I don't know whether I need to question the witness about the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you have anything to add concerning paragraph 2.1 in connection with this French member of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Exhibit 3D1048, paragraph 2.7. It's on page 2 in the Serbian version and probably page 2 in English, but I don't have it here. I don't have the English version. It's rather brief. I apologise for the interpreters once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.7: "Through a reliable source information had arrived that members of the verification mission, mostly persons from the American team to a large extent are providing logistical assistance to the terrorists, to whom they regularly forward the information they have on movements of the police and army and the actions taken, so that the terrorist groups have time to withdraw or come to the aid of other terrorist groups who are in conflict. Also, information is available that they have been instructed by the verifiers to reduce their activities for now up to the meeting in Rambouillet on the 15th of March of this year, so as not to be blamed for a deterioration of the situation and a possible failure of the meeting." I will also read paragraph 2.8, which says: "According to operative information of the security organs of the 14th, several cases of forwarding information on the movements, strength, and activities of the VJ and MUP have been registered for the verifiers of the regional centre Pristina by correspondence of the terrorist organisation, the so-called KLA, which indicates that they are in league with the terrorists -- that there is a league between the terrorists and the Kosovo Verification Mission."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two questions arising out of that. Paragraph 2.7, just answer this question yes or no, do you know the identity of the source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, but it can be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My second question is: What was done at the highest level of the state to raise with the KVM concern about their alleged collaboration with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a Federal Commission for the implementation of the agreement which had been achieved with the OSCE, or rather, the verification mission. This information of ours - and there is much more of this - was summarized by us until the regular information we sent to users in the top state leadership so that they were aware of all these problems. But I don't know what steps they took to deal with this. Our task was only to inform them, to indicate what the problems were; what they did about them, I couldn't say. All I know is they were informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gajic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have to ask a question. Now, this -- close your -- this appear to be a serious allegation when a mission which is supposed to be neutral, it is alleged, was trying to be in league with the -- one of the parties. Now, was there a public protest? Because a very senior person from the government was trying to cooperate with the KVM and he was the vice-president. So was there a public protest vociferously speaking of this sort of conspiracy or league of these two against yourselves? Because merely if it was only buried in documents that's another thing, but it ought to be if that was an issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. As far as I know, the chairman of this commission, Mr. Sainovic, did have a meeting in connection with the problems observed in cooperation with the verification mission. I do not know whether this problem was touched on. Let me add one thing, Your Honours, by your leave, something I witnessed which is not found in these documents. On the 26th of August, 1998, I was in Kosovo, and on that occasion members of the 14th counter-intelligence group in the town of Orahovac confiscated several thousand statements taken by -- or taken from Albanians. All these statements had the OSCE heading. They were formalised. There was identifying data in Albanian and a statement. When we looked at these statements and had them translated from Albanian, we found that they all followed the same pattern. We tried to check what this was about, and we found that all over Kosovo a survey of the Albanian population had been made, so to speak. Some sort of evidence was being gathered about the difficult situation and mistreatment of the Albanian people. We then went further and tried to check to see whether the OSCE had also surveyed Serbs, Montenegrins, and other non-Albanians in order to get an objective picture of the situation, and we found not a single case of that. I tried --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, you've departed completely from the question that you were being asked. Please confine yourself to what you're being asked about. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I proceed, let me draw attention to the testimony of John Clark, a member of the KVM, Exhibit 6D106 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, we don't want witnesses here prompted by references to what others have said. You can make your submissions about that in due course. We're listening at the moment to the knowledge of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. 3D1052, paragraph 2.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, please tell us, what information did you have about this event?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this confirms what we have been saying so far. It's about the engagement of the members of the KVM in bringing in food and assisting in the care of wounded members of the KLA in an improvised hospital. It doesn't say here precisely which improvised hospital because probably the location could not be precisely established.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And Exhibit 3D1053, paragraph 2.3. This is a report of the 16th of March, 1999. General, what did this information mean to you, that members of the KVM insisted on new pseudonyms and codes, numbers, for locations where members of the terrorist groups were?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means that the circumstances at the time changed and what was about to happen, the events we just spoke about -- we have just been speaking about, and it confirms that these contacts were, or rather, that these contacts amounted to cooperation and mutual assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This document is dated the 16th of March, 1999, which is just a week before the attack of NATO on Yugoslavia and is there any connection, in your view?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my view there is a connection because these were secrecy measures to have the codes changed, to protect the locations and the activities. This means that some kind of confidential links had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Your Honours do not have any questions, we will round off this topic and conclude these documents concerning KLA activities. I would now like the General to comment on 3D685, page 65, line 9, I know I didn't say, about documents concerning the KVM and the KLA, I omitted to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you recognise the document before you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, General, whether your administration participated in compiling this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one segment of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is the assessment of the intelligence and security situation and danger to the security of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have page 3, both in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell Their Honours, these are the contents, but can you tell Their Honours what part of this document your administration participated in compiling?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 2: "Influence of the internal factor," and 2.1 and 2.2: "Situation in Kosovo and Metohija" and "situation in the Raska-Polimlje district." 2.3 was done by the administration for morale and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the text on page 12, and in English it's page 13, paragraph 4. Could we scroll down in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the document speaks for itself so we need not go into detail, but what does this show in relation to some of the information we saw in the previous documents?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a more complex assessment of the security and intelligence situation focusing on Kosovo and Metohija and the Rasko-Polimsa 12.29.01 area. That area was focused on because there was a latent threat that the violence might spread there from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's stick to Kosovo and Metohija now, General.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the next page, please. B/C/S page 13, English page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you have in front of you the assessment of the KLA forces based on the intelligence the army had at its disposal in February 1999 when this document was compiled?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the gist of all the intelligence gathered by the counter-intelligence service and other services that we were able to obtain by exchanging information related to terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Since we have numbers and strength of some of the brigades here, could you please comment on just the last passage that starts with the words: "The operational zone commands ..."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had had rather reliable information at that time that the first recording of all Albanian men of military age was carried out in 1997, as early as then. And now, in light of the previous events, they again went to update their records. All the staffs made and updated records of all Albanian men of military age for their voluntary or forcible mobilisation in order to set up new units and staffs or to reinforce the existing ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in the footnote, or rather, could you please tell me, what does it mean, which makes it possible for them to increase their forces over a very short period of time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely because they had all records of men of military age, Albanian men of military age, and the measures they took to mobilise them voluntarily or forcibly, as we mentioned in my previous evidence and there is more information about that, they were able to increase their forces, the strength of their forces, substantially over a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the footnote of this document - and the Trial Chamber will have the opportunity to peruse it in more detail, we have a statistical overview of the incidents in 1998. General, I wanted to ask you a question, the Yugoslav Army, did it have any reason to overestimate the strength or the danger in that period of time or to falsely represent the number and gravity of incidents?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think. I think that these are quite realistic data.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Was this document meant for external use, was it going to be sent to somebody outside of the system, an external agent who perhaps needed to be shown some data that were not actually realistic, that did not exist?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I know how this document was drafted. Now, whether some information contained therein was used in communication or contact with any external factors, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General Obradovic explained to us how this document was put together, now I'm asking you about this portion that you yourself drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now could we go to page 16, paragraph 2 of the English text and page 15, paragraph 2 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment very briefly on what the Army of Yugoslavia still considered to be the key problem? You see paragraph 2, right there at the top.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean "all this shows"?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No. "Securing the state border ..."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The state border with Albania was the constant problem in this respect because Albania was the main logistics base for the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me interrupt you. We've heard evidence about that, so could you please tell me, at the time when this document was drafted did the Army of Yugoslavia, in considering the problems it had with the KLA, what was defined as the biggest problem in solving the issue related to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of the key problems was to cut off the supplies for the -- the illegal channels for smuggling in of terrorists and weapons from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And when it says at this time they have the appropriate quantities of all light and infantry weapons, MES, what's that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mines and explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As well as anti-aircraft weapons, what does it mean, "appropriate quantities"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that some basic units were well-supplied with all those and some elements there where the KLA was stationed, and that for the most part, in particular Metohija, in the Dukagjin Operative Zone and in Drenica, they did not have sufficient quantities of those things and they were preparing for a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that their efforts to procure weapons did not follow the mobilisation, the increased mobilisation efforts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they never had any problems with money.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now let me draw your attention to the last passage in this chapter which reads as follows: "Because of systematic terrorist attacks, killings, abductions, pressures and threats against the Serbian and Montenegrin population, there is a realistic danger of those people organising resistance on their own, which may further complicate the existing situation in Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, my question to you is: Those people arming and organising themselves to put up resistance, this was a problem for the army, not something that it supported?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what you say is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, what was your fear expressed in this assessment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were afraid that the Serbs and Montenegrins and others who were, objectively speaking, in a very difficult situation under constant pressure to move out and their lives were at considerable risk, we were afraid that they might take up arms. There were arms about. It was not difficult to get them, at least infantry weapons. We were afraid that they would take up arms and that there would be clashes because the Albanian villages, the Albanian villages had already been armed by the KLA and they had some Territorial Defence units set up to defend their villages but they could also be used in an attack. And there could follow some inter-ethnic clashes, and we are indeed pointing to this risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, you're not the first person to tell us that the border had not been secured. Do you know why that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think, Judge Bonomy, that the main problem was lack of troops. We didn't have enough troops, and this problem was stressed several times. And quite objectively speaking this was not easy to solve. Secondly, as far as I can remember, the Pristina Corps command in 1999, during the war in fact, did an analysis and they found that -- I think that this is correct, that there were 175 locations where the state border could be crossed illegally and where weapons, ammunition, and terrorists could be smuggled in aside from the control posts, border posts, and it was physically impossible to control all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even though you could identify the number of places that such crossings could take place? We appreciate it's a very difficult terrain that forms the border, but that, in a sense, also reduces the potential places for crossing the border and you've been able to confirm that there was a recognised number of those. Was it not possible to have -- would it not have been possible to man these sufficiently to secure the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, your conclusion is quite proper, and measures were, indeed, taken in the course of the anti-terrorist operation, the main channels leading from Albania to Metohija and further into the depth. That was a problem. When these channels were cut off, people from the KLA top said that getting weapons from Albania became a big problem for them because the channels had been cut off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gajic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in response to Judge Bonomy's question you said that the Pristina Corps command did an analysis, and it says here that you said that it was during the war. I assume that you meant it was done just before the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I'm not quite sure, but I know that a detailed analysis was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We will be calling other evidence on this issue so I don't think it would be controversial in any way, but I just wanted to clear this up. General, do you know that just before the war the border belt was, indeed, extended on the border facing Albania?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that it was done in May or July, that it was extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not quite sure how we're set for time. Is the break coming up now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Is the answer at line 10 the one you anticipated?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you about 1999. Do you know that in 1999 on the eve of the war the border belt was extended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one brief question. General, in your statement you dealt with the removal of General Dimitrijevic and the appointment of General Farkas. I want to ask you, is it true that there was an option that envisaged General Dimitrijevic still remaining as the head of the service?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was offered the post of the assistant to the federal minister of defence for the coordination of the military intelligence and counter-intelligence service of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When did General Farkas take over?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was stated that as of the 24th of March he was the new head of the security administration. I was told that by General Dimitrijevic, and on the 25th of March I submitted my report, I was one of the people who did so, to General Farkas. Other people followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And is it true that General Dimitrijevic remained in the service in the VJ for some sometime afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because according to the law and regulations, there is a certain period of time for the handover of duty. Once I and my subordinates reported to General Farkas, this was not over. So he and General Farkas remained there for a while doing this handover.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honours, that this is a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may just raise something before we pause. There have been a lot of leading questions earlier. There was no -- probably no need to object because much of it was in the statement, much of what was being led was in the statement or in the documents. However, now we are moving away from the documents and the statement and the last set of questions have been entirely leading, but you Captain -- I can't pick them up in time. The witness is saying "yes," by the time I'm getting the translation, so I ask if we are moving out of matters that are in the statement that is in evidence already that we could refrain from leading the witness because there's no possibility to object before the witness answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. I'm not entirely in agreement with you that that was a series of leading questions; however, it's important to observe --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- The comment made, Mr. Visnjic. Thank you. We have to break now for an hour, Mr. Gajic, so could you again leave the courtroom and we'll see you again at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.48 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, now I would like us to move to a different period, that's the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like 3D584 to be shown to the witness, please, page 2, both in the English and in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in your statement in the sections that relate to your function explained where you were and what you did at the beginning of the aggression or the attack of the NATO alliance against Yugoslavia. General, do you recognise the document that's now in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly what this is all about. Other people will testify about the way in which this document was drafted and so on, but very briefly could you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the minutes from the reporting or from the briefing to the chief of Supreme Command Staff. The date is the 31st of March, 1999, it started at 8.30, and I think that it's actually a mistake because it ended at 2200 hours. And all those persons who were present there are clearly listed with their functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. Could we please move on to page 2 of this document, it's both in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The question is: You attended this briefing and you, yourself, submitted a report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here that the deputy chief of the security administration is present, that would be me. That's what I was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the middle of this page I see your name. Could you please tell me, you reported certain data you had about NATO and the sabotage terrorist groups, and by that they mean the KLA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What information did you have on the 31st of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we already had intelligence that intense training was underway in the KLA. They were undergoing training in the centres in Albania. We also learned, however - this was operational intelligence - that such training was going on in Macedonia. We also had information we received from KLA prisoner whom we interrogated that in the course of the training of the KLA in the centres of Albania that the officers from some NATO country -- some NATO-member countries were also involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P1475.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: After those meetings did General Ojdanic issue any orders or give any tasks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after each briefing General Ojdanic assigned tasks in a very accurate manner and often there -- in most cases there would also be deadlines set for the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P1475.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And could you please comment on it briefly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 2nd of April, 1999, it's a preventive order, as indicated in paragraph 1. It deals with the treatment of the members of the enemy armed forces who surrender or laid down their arms, how they're to be treated, and they should be treated in accordance with the provisions of international law of war and the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move on to another document, 3D721, that would be page 1 in the B/C/S, the last two pages, and in English that would be page 1, the last four lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we have another briefing, the date is the 3rd of April, 1999, as indicated on this document you were again present?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This time you tell the Chief of General Staff and his collegium, if we may call it that, about certain problems that occur in the territory. You had already received information that some crimes had been committed; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this report contains very important information and that's about the purported 500.000 refugees. We had this information, and General Krga I think presented some similar data regarding the number of refugees in Kosovo and that figure was placed around 500.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 2, that is the intervention by General Krga.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your report begins on page 1, continues into page 2 --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the Pentagon?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, I mean the problem with the paramilitary formations. You say here that: "We have information that they were volunteers," and so on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the initial data indicating that there were paramilitaries operating in Kosovo, but we were unable to identify them, who was there. We did some research on the orders of the chief of Supreme Command Staff, who insisted that it be determined whether there were any paramilitaries there, and particularly whether any of them relied on the Yugoslav Army. So this was the initial raw intelligence that we had and we went on to verify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that on the very same day the Chief of General Staff on the basis of this information related to the problems related to volunteers and paramilitaries issue any orders that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's plainly building up to a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Your Honour. [Interpretation] That would be Exhibit 1477, P1477, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a preventive order again. It is related to the processing of those who committed crimes, as indicated in paragraph 1, and then in paragraph 2 it is further stated that the chief of the Supreme Command Staff who signed this order orders that conscripts, soldiers, and volunteers who committed any crimes should be treated in the same way or any acts that are in contravention of the Law of War and Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When was this order issued?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 3rd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and counsel please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, another warning there about overlapping questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at the next Exhibit, that's P1476. This is again an order from the Supreme Command Staff dated the 3rd of April, 1999. Could you please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it on the screen yet. Yet. This is again an order, a preventive order, confirming what I have just said, that the chief of the Supreme Command Staff accords the same treatment to the enemy, to the friend and foe when it comes to investigating any acts that are in contravention of the international law of war and Geneva Conventions. This is about gathering physical evidence, about the use of inhumane weapons by NATO in the course of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: By that time, General, was there already some evidence that NATO was using - I'm not going to say "unlawful," - but I'm going to say inhumane weapons in combat?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was about cluster bombs and about depleted uranium. We were dealing with that at the Supreme Command level and at the order of the Supreme Command Staff a presentation was done to acquaint people with it because many of us did not know all the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see Defence Exhibit 3D482. This is an order of the Supreme Command Staff dated the 16th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please just comment briefly on it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is again a warning order, a warning in fact. Some problems had been noticed regarding the conduct in the course of combat operations on our side that are in contravention of the provisions of the international law of war and the chief of the Supreme Command Staff considered that there was a need to warn all the subordinate commands, that those isolated incidents could not be allowed to spread, and that all the perpetrators should be treated energetically in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 2 in particular of this page -- of this document, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 3 we have the special warning binding the commands and all the professional organs, including the security organs and the military police units, to prevent all forms of crime - and it is specified what forms of crime are considered - because this was shaping up into a problem. The chief of the Supreme Command Staff is warning everybody that they should act strenuously and vigorously.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When the chief of Supreme Command Staff issues such an order, whom is it sent to and what happens with such an order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is issued to the subordinate strategic commands and other commands at their level.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And who would that be in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Army, the commander of the 3rd Army --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise, I will. The commander of the 3rd Army pursuant to their order will draft his own order, and in this order he will refer to the order of the Supreme Command Staff. This order would then be sent to his subordinate units, that would be the Pristina Corps. The Pristina Corps commander in his turn writes his own order, perhaps adding some elements that have been noted, that are specific, referring again to the previous orders, and then this order goes on to his units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at P1454, page 1 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only the English version. It's okay now. May I comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would like you to.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is precisely what I said. The commander of the 3rd Army, this order from the Supreme Command Staff was dated the 16th of April, and now the 3rd Army commander issues an order on the 17th with his signature to the commander of the Pristina Corps referring to the warning issued by the chief of the Supreme Command dated the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please look at P1672.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from the 3rd Army command sent to his subordinates ordering, stating - you can see that in the preamble - that problems had been noted with -- involving weapons, uniformed people with arms moving around the outside of the area of responsibility using their weapons in contravention of the regulations and referring to the order of the chief of Supreme Command Staff he orders measuring to be taken to prevent that. That is to say that what preceded was an order by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now have a look at Exhibit P1688.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a preventive order yet again and its author is the sector for logistics, and it was signed as well by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and it has to do with military conscripts. It was noted that some of them had psychiatric problems; that is to say that this was something that the commissions for admitting recruits had done wrong, volunteers, conscripts. Obviously the medical commissions fell short of what they were supposed to do, so that was supposed to be redressed. Let me just add one more thing, in the previous order as well as in this order, at the end it is always stated that regarding all measures reports should be sent through regular or extraordinary reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you to look at 3D483. General, please give us your comment regarding this order dated the 10th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an order dated the 10th of May, 1999, and - how should I put this? - it's a warning, actually. It is an order but it's also a warning. It has to do with problems in terms of violations of international humanitarian law and law of war and the Geneva Conventions. In the reports that came in, these problems were noted and the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command reacted, and in paragraph 3 he makes it incumbent upon all commanders and all commanding officers to make personal measures to prevent violations of international laws of war and the Geneva Conventions and that every officer bears personal responsibility if he does not take regular measures, properly measures in accordance with the law with respect to all perpetrators of crimes or disciplinary infractions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in the Serbian version --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we actually show page 3 to the witness in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it's in the English version of this document, too. There were probably some difficulties in terms of translation. Could you just tell the Judges what accompanied this order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along with this previous order that I commented upon, there was this attachment concerning criminal liability for war crimes and other grave violations of international law of war and crimes against humanity and international law. So there are certain provisions here where it is stated what the law of war implies and it is clearly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So these are provisions of various laws or the Geneva Conventions, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we have dealt with this set of preventive orders issued by the Chief of General Staff. As for the briefing on the 31st of March, you said to the Chief of General Staff, or rather, your drew his attention to the problem of law violations on the part of certain volunteers. I would like to ask you to look at Defence Exhibit 3D481. General, you saw this document while preparing for your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your comments regarding this order, but only from the aspect of security because other witnesses are going to testify about this document later.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order dated the 14th of April that relates to the acceptance and distribution of volunteers in the Army of Yugoslavia. The first order about this was issued on the 2nd of April, 1999, but then this order overrules that one. This is very precise and very specific. It is stated exactly what the centres are through which volunteers are received and taken in. What is to say -- what I'm trying to say is there are three centres --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just from the point of view of security, General, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What else is regulated is that in each one of these centres there are going to be security organs who in line with their own duties they will actively take part in receiving these volunteers and processing them from a security point of view and ultimately assigning them to specific units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just slowly, please. Now go on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirdly what is regulated is the question of their training, their arming, and specifically where they are being assigned. It is stated that they cannot be assigned all together to one unit. Not more than five volunteers can be in an individual unit. I think that was very important because until then there had been quite a few problems in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I'd like to ask you to look at Defence Exhibit 3D587. Sorry, I beg your pardon. 3D729, page 3 of this document, please, in Serbian and in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a briefing to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command dated the 12th of April, 1999. The document shows that the witness took part in this briefing, but I wish to ask him about a specific point on this page, and that is point 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you give us your comments. First of all, who is issuing instructions here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And could you give us your comments with regard to point 3?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't find this very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Look at the bottom of the page, will you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Right. The chief of the Supreme Command Staff, since it was pointed out during these briefings that there were problems with paramilitary formations, so the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, as I have already said, always at the end of a briefing he issues very specific tasks, often with special deadlines. He asked us for information on paramilitary formations, what it was that we specifically had on paramilitary formations, what it was that we had established actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please look at 3D586, pages 1 and 2. Your remarks start on page 1 and continue on page 2. The situation is similar in the English text. General, could you please look at what you said on page 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then could he please see page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So could you please give us your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But may I just deal with this first sentence on page 1, please. So on orders of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command at every subsequent briefing at the very outset we would have to report on what we had done in terms of the realisation of our previous tasks, the tasks that we had been assigned the previous briefing. So now you see here in my own remarks what is underway is the completion of the task received at the previous briefing, and that is what everybody was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. While we are still on page 1 there is some activity that is referred to concerning the discovery of alleged mass graves in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Could you tell the Trial Chamber something about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we had information from the media mostly, from journalists, because I'd like to say already then in Belgrade a press centre had been established where there were about 700 accredited journalists, both from home and abroad. And there was quite a bit of -- well, perhaps I shouldn't say misinformation, but there were various references to various situations. We tried to check things out as much as we could, but I believe that nevertheless I should point out that that was going on but that we couldn't really ascertain anything. I would say that this was media manipulation. I can't remember now who the journalists involved were. At the time I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could he please have a look at the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We see here on the top of page 2, we see your remarks continued.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And now what had to do with General Ojdanic's orders in respect of paramilitary formations from the previous briefings, that is.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand your question. What is referred to here is Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did General Ojdanic at one of the previous briefings issue instructions to you that information be submitted to him on the existence of paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now what kind of information you gave him and what it pertained to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We gave him information, although we were still checking this information out, but we got some rather specific information about the engagement of the paramilitary formation of the Skorpions commanded by Slobo Medic, Boca. However, this information that was presented to the Chief of Staff was still being double-checked. And in mid-May, we established the full accuracy of this information. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I'm looking at -- what we have here is the formation of paramilitary formations that are within the MUP of Montenegro. What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were following the situation in Montenegro too because there was a spillover in a way in Kosovo and Metohija because Montenegro was a transit area and so on and so forth. So through our own operatives we established with quite a degree of reliability that what was under way there was the establishment of three paramilitary formations. One was the liberation army of Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We don't need to go through all the details.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three paramilitary organisations, and we even discovered who the organisers were and even identified a number of the members of these paramilitary organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit 3D587, the Serbian text again page 1, the bottom of page 1, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a document we've already seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 587, Your Honour, I thought that we had seen 586.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we haven't seen this document yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D587.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This has to do with briefing on the 15th of April -- sorry, the 16th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could I have it back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the General saw this first page where his remarks begin, could you please display page 2 for him. And -- yes, the English is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, tell me, what information did you have available on the 16th of April, 1999, in connection with paramilitary activities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two things. One has to do with Loznica and the establishment of a paramilitary formation and in connection with that paramilitary formation this piece of information that about 400 Albanians were liquidated. Allegedly this paramilitary formation did this. According to this initial information, the formation had previously been in Kosovo and was now preparing to go to Kosovo again. We checked this information, but it proved to be incorrect. What was correct, however, was that they were carrying out certain preparations to go to Kosovo and we informed the state security about what we had learned, and they most probably responded because we were monitoring this situation and that group did not go to Kosovo. The second point I raised at the briefing was that in Belgrade a volunteer unit was being formed to do with Kosovo. This was a group of men originating from the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Republika Srpska who had been members of the paramilitary formations there, and in Belgrade they kept in touch and they talked about going to Kosovo. They would argue and then they would make it up, and then they would say they were going, and then they would say they weren't going; and we were monitoring the situation and they did not go. Afterwards when we checked we found that they had not gone to Kosovo. Some individuals might have gone because there were individuals who went there purely to loot. There was a lot of looting in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now turn to page 4 of the text in Serbian and also page 4 of the text in English of this same document, 3D587.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, on that day, the 16th of April, 1999, you received certain orders from the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on point 6 on this page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This -- well, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command was not fully satisfied with the information we presented to him, and he insisted that the security administration should be more active and establish the facts. He was especially interested in whether there were paramilitaries, either in or in connection with the army and whether there were any paramilitaries in all of Kosovo. So here he is reiterating this task and insisting that we should be far more active in checking this and establishing the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask about this. I find it very strange that the army can't say one way or another whether there are paramilitaries operating in any given area. Do you not find it strange that that is difficult to establish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not unusual. First of all the people who got together as members of paramilitary formations, if they were not linked to any of the security forces down there they did it in the greatest possible secrecy and their main aim was theft and looting as well as robbery I would add.
