There was violence as well. These were very closed circles. These people originated from Croatia, many of them, they had been through the war and the paramilitaries there. They had been to Bosnia-Herzegovina, they had embarked on a life of crime, and they were very cautious. So it was very difficult to penetrate those circles and establish the true situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've given us a lot of information today about the activities of the KLA and the KVM, and yet here there doesn't seem to be any concrete evidence of ever proving criminal activity on the part of the -- of any paramilitary organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we established was first in connection with the army in 99.9 per cent of the cases there were no paramilitary formations in the army but there was several linked to the MUP. I mentioned Slobodan Medic, Boca, and the Skorpions; there was Arkan's unit; and there was one unit from Republika Srpska, the Wolves from the Drina. That's what we established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what had you established had been done by the Skorpions in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We established that on the 31st of March in Podujevo they committed a crime. They killed ten children and two grown-up civilians, two adults. They were brought back to Kosovo to Prolom Banja, but they turned up in Kosovo again. And this was a topic of discussion and we'll come to that at a meeting with Slobodan Milosevic on the 17th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What did you establish Arkan's group did in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We established that in the centre in Kosovo Polje there was some sort of centre there for the reception of these volunteers. They committed a crime. They killed two elderly persons, a husband and wife. And as we were told - and this came from the state security - proceedings were instituted against them, they were under investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's it, two elderly deaths?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what we knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what did you establish had been done in Kosovo by the Wolves from the Drina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were under the command of Nedeljko Karisak known as Legenda who had been the commander of special anti-terrorist units of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We established that they were in Kosovo Polje, but we were unable to establish what their activities were, what was going on there, and whether they had caused any trouble or not because this was not within the purview of the military security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could bodies like that operate without their conduct or their acts being established, without them being protected in some way by either the MUP or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer to this question is that in the case of these three paramilitary formations they did not go through the procedure according to the orders of the chief of the Main Staff of the 16th of April, 1999, concerning the reception, processing, and sending of volunteers. Had they applied in the centre, they would not have been accepted as volunteers and they would not have been sent to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question is rather different. How is it they can operate in Kosovo without the cover of either the MUP or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand your question. According to our information, which I believe is correct, all of them, Boca, Arkan, and the Drina Wolves wore SAJ units, MUP units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Exhibit 3D592, please, page 1 in both versions. Also a report of the 22nd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: According to this order of the Chief of the General Staff of the 16th of April, you provided some more information at this briefing concerning paramilitary formations. Could you please take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down on the Serbian version, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go into that, line 7 on page 93, my note of that answer was that each of these groups wore MUP uniforms. Is that consistent with the answer given by the witness in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said both SAJ and MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. It was only translated in English as "MUP," but that's helpful. Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I also thought that there was another element to the answer I heard translated that the witness said that they wore MUP -- they wore SAJ/MUP uniforms. That's what I thought I heard but I might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in English we certainly heard uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, why not ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you clarify that, Mr. Gajic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, SAJ uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you simply say SAJ uniforms or did you say SAJ and MUP uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said MUP because the SAJ is part of MUP, but in actual fact it's SAJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at this briefing, if you are referring to this bit about Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although we had provided specific information at some of the previous briefings, we continued to monitor this and we established that there were not only members of paramilitary formations coming from Montenegro but that they were participants of the war in Krajina because the border between Republika Srpska and Montenegro was completely open because of the black-marketeering that went on and the smuggling and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English page 4, Serbian page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Ojdanic made a comment and gave an order. Can you tell us what this is about, just wait a little bit, it will appear on the screen, it's point 6.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this referred to us in the security administration. It's not quite clear to me. I don't remember what document is in question, but here it says the main commander in the area, which means that nothing can be done without the knowledge of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, are you aware that the Army of Yugoslavia issued a document called: "Instructions for officers and fighters"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the briefing I think of the 18th of April, 1999, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff ordered General Curcin, who was in the operations staff sector to prepare and make 1.300 copies of these documents, on the basis of which each soldier would have certain provisions built in and that this should be sent to the Pristina Corps. And as far as I know, General Pavkovic and General Lazarevic, pursuant to this, made sure that each soldier was given the most important provisions of the Geneva Conventions and the international laws of war and that both the commanding officers and the men were trained in this respect. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document, 3D593.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the strength of the Pristina Corps 1300?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because it was not possible to make a copy for each and every soldier, but pursuant to the commander of the 3rd Army the most important provisions, referring to certain points in the international laws of war and the Geneva Conventions, had to be -- had to be communicated to each soldier so that each soldier would know about it and every commander, every leader, was given these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, to clarify once again, so the entire brochure was instructions for commanders, and soldiers were given only excerpts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D593, B/C/S page 1, English page 1. It's the 23rd of April, 1999, it's a briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you are giving two pieces of information here to the Supreme Command Staff referring to Montenegro. Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was referring to paramilitaries and crime. I'm providing information about the paramilitaries in Krusevac, that's a place in the south of Serbia. The Serbian liberation army, which we as security officers observed and monitored, we documented their activities, we submitted a criminal report, and they were all sentenced. The leader of that paramilitary formation had the same last name as me, although we're not related, his name was Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But this group has nothing to do with Kosovo; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only insofar as they were preparing to go to Kosovo. They were preparing weapons and they were also threatening the commander of the 3rd Army, General Pavkovic, saying they would liquidate him. What was your other question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The next piece of information that you gave down the chain of command, property-related crime is being prevented. What does that mean? Stable situation, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did have this kind of problem, property-related crime, especially arms and ammunition. This was a permanent problem, and then we presented all of this information to the command in order to have measures taken by them within their jurisdiction, and these measures inter alia were to have arms, ammunition, explosives, ordnance be placed in more secure storage and to work hard on finding the perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P1902. Your Honour, it was admitted into evidence twice, once as P1902 and once as P1490, lest there be any confusion I would like to draw your attention to that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, now after all this information that you submitted to the Supreme Command Staff, what is it that we have before us now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order dated the 26th of April, General Ojdanic, the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, where he insists yet again on checking on the presence of paramilitary formations and their activity and he orders measures that have to be taken in order to eliminate them from the area of Kosovo and Metohija, starting with disarming and then also Prosecution in accordance with the law. Tasks are given there what commands should do and what security organs should do with regard to that matter. Also under number 4 a report is asked for in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, in your statement -- well, we're not going to go back to it in detail, but I would just like to take you to the next time-frame that I would like you to deal with. You stated that the chief of the security administration went to Kosovo in the beginning of May or the end of April, I can't remember exactly. Can you tell me what the reasons were why General Farkas made this trip?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Geza Farkas stayed in Kosovo-Metohija from the 5th until the 6th. There were three basic reasons for that. The first reason was, if I can put it that way, was a regular visit because it was our practice to see all security organs during the course of the year, not practice, but this is what was regularly done, and the previous one took place on the 3rd and 4th of March where I was on the inspection team --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, General, let's go back to General Farkas, why did he go?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a regular visit. Secondly, due to this knowledge that we had regarding paramilitary formations, well the situation was not quite clear to us. So the third reason was that there were some problems related to the engagement of the military police that was not always in accordance with the law and other regulations and, generally speaking, to look at the work of the security organs with regard to current issues and all important issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Defence Exhibit 3D606 be shown, please. This is the briefing of the 6th of May, 1999, the English text page 3, the B/C/S text page 3. Page 3, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you see at the bottom of the page in B/C/S, it says: "Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command," concluding remarks and tasks. And the first question that was put by General Ojdanic was whether there were any paramilitary formations in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he asked and my answer was, regrettably, yes. I talked to General Farkas, he returned on the 6th, I had spoken to him and I had initial information on what it was that his findings were down there. We spoke briefly on the telephone but he told me that there were major problems down there and inter alia he told me that there were problems relating to paramilitary [Realtime transcript read in error "apartment"] formations. However, that on the following day, that is to say on the 7th, at the morning collegium meeting he would tell me about it in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What did General Ojdanic specifically ask you to do, General?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked for specificity, if I can put it that way. That is what he says here. We're not going to do anything through making general conclusions. He really wanted to have this cleared up, and he said that if there were such persons in Kosovo that they should be expelled, that legal measures should be taken, so he was very precise on that as always. So what was going on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a second. Your Honour, page 99, line 14, I think it might be important to know what was said there, I'm sure it wasn't apartment formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it was paramilitary formations --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me see, yes, paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us briefly now what it was that happened during the course of the following few days after that meeting that was held in the evening on the 6th of May at 8.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the morning of the 7th of May, we had a collegium of the chief of administration for security, and General Farkas presented in the briefest possible terms what his observations were from his visit in Kosovo and Metohija. He gave an assessment concerning the work of the security organs and he said that the security organs were working well; however, that there were problems down there. And he just mentioned them one by one. He did not go into any detail because he didn't really have time to do all that -- and he said --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Visnjic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When he was in Kosovo, that's what I am talking about, and he said specifically that there were paramilitary formations, that there was looting down there, that there were rapes, and that there were crimes, that there were many thefts. That was the core of the matter. Then we talked about that in terms of what should be done further and the proposal made to him was to familiarise the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command straight away. He indeed spoke to him on the telephone and he probably gave him this kind of information briefly. I am not aware of the details, but I know that the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command ordered that on the 13th of May we meet, that a meeting be held at his office, and that on the 13th of May at that time this day was the holiday of the security services that was still being observed at that time. So we came there, General Geza, General Vasiljevic, and I. General Geza provided information to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command roughly along these lines, that there were problems down there, and that this was the first time that we heard of those problems in terms of what they actually were, that there was crime there as well, and that it would be a good thing for it to be discussed truly and to see what should be done further. We suggested on the basis of these remarks -- well, then the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command said, I am going to inform the president about that now and I think it would be a good thing for a meeting to be held. He called Milosevic and told him briefly that there were problems down there, that Geza was down there and that there were serious problems down there. And I think that he mentioned that crimes had been committed too and it would be a good thing to have a special meeting held. Milosevic said to him on the 17th of May at 0930 hours, Meeting at my place. So we were supposed to be there, we from the army and representatives of the MUP, too. Then General Ojdanic immediately on the telephone there while we were preparatory called General Pavkovic, and after saying, Hello Nebojsa, what's up, are there any problems down there? And he mentioned the problem of crimes. And General Pavkovic answered that there were problems and that he had documentation about that and that he had everything. General Ojdanic then ordered on the 16th of May at 2000 hours meeting at the command post and that all this documentation he should bring along with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to show you Exhibit 3D1055. General, tell us, what is this about, the 13th of May, 1999, is the date of this document, so that's the same day when you had a meeting with General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me. We took along this information about the activities of the paramilitary formation of Slobodan Medic, Boca, and we gave it to General Ojdanic. He read it and he said that he would give this information to Milosevic too. Everything that we informed him about was based on this, so that was the problem and I don't want to repeat everything about the meeting that was scheduled for 8.00 in the evening and going to see Milosevic and so on, everything that I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, can you tell us just briefly you were present at the meetings on the 16th of May and on the 17th of May. Can you describe for us briefly what happened at these meetings? General Vasiljevic already testified about that, so let us not be too extensive on this. Can you just give us some brief information about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of May we met at the command post. General Ojdanic was present, General Pavkovic, General Vasiljevic, General Geza, and I. An introduction was made by General Ojdanic. He pointed out a few things there. As for war crimes that every case had to be urgently investigated and documented, and if it is established that somebody had committed a war crime they should be arrested straight away. That is literally what he said, Criminal report, arrest, straight to court. If it belongs to the military judiciary, then it should be resolved urgently, but if it is from the jurisdiction of the civilian courts, then the civilian judiciary should take this upon themselves to resolve the matter, whereas we in terms of resolving these problems related to war crimes and other crimes that are in contravention of --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, everything that is against international law --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You haven't really slowed down. Would you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I really have that problem. He said that as far as war crimes were concerned, nothing should be forgiven, no one should be forgiven, and that war crimes and everything else that is in contravention of international laws of war and the Geneva Conventions could compromise the Army of Yugoslavia. He also said the MUP and the state and that we should not allow that to happen. As for paramilitaries and volunteers, he also said that every case has to be investigated and things should be clarified and measures taken. Again he stated that on the following day, on the 17th, we'd have a meeting at Milosevic's and that this was a preparatory meeting. He said that Geza had been down there and he said briefly what it was that Geza had seen down there, and then he gave the floor to General Pavkovic. General Pavkovic had all of that documentation, and I have just referred to a few things that he had spoken about. He said that in Prolom Banja he had a contact with Boca. He couldn't remember his name and surname straight away, and he said that this person belonged to some paramilitary formation. And he said that Boca told him during that conversation that he had not been in Kosovo; however, he said, he lied to me. Because afterwards when speaking to General Djakovic, and he was head of the operations department in the 3rd Army, he said to him that he had indeed been in Kosovo and that Rodja had called them, that is Djordjevic, nicknamed Rodja, and they should be engaged in Kosovo when some most complex and most difficult tasks are to be carried out. That is what he said about Medic. Secondly, he spoke about the problem of war crimes and that there were a few problems related to that. One problem has to do with the crimes committed, because the army has one set of information, the MUP had another set of data, and the truth is somewhere midway.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just slow down, General, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will. He said that as for what had been investigated to date had to do with the figure of 271. And as far as the MUP was concerned, the figure is 326.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on. What happened about Boca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think in late April, until the 10th of May, they were there and then they were expelled from Kosovo. What happened after that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does that -- how does that tie in with this idea that we will take action against everybody who's suspected of a war crime? Why was nothing done about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not within the competency of the military judiciary, but rather the civilian courts which -- well, they were to -- they had to be arrested and they had to be reported, and the civilian courts should have dealt with that. The army did what it was up to the army to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I thought you told us that General Ojdanic said that as for paramilitaries and volunteers, every case has to be investigated. Things should be clarified and measures taken. Did that not apply to Boca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it did, but the army dealt with what was within the competence of the military and the military courts. But matters that had to do with the civilian judiciary, that was up for the civilian judiciary to deal with. Boca was within the competence of the civilian judiciary, not the military courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be so, but why -- you've just told us what General Ojdanic said about paramilitaries, that you should be taking action against them. Why would he do that if you had no power to do anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I did not express myself well or perhaps we misunderstand one another. He just said in general what had to be done in relation to paramilitaries as well as volunteers who committed some illegal actions, but each had to deal with matters within their own competence. If it was a volunteer and he had been dismissed and then he came under the competence of the civilian judiciary, he would have to be the -- proceedings would have to be before the civilian judiciary. If someone left the army and became a civilian, then the case had to be handed to the civilian courts, and the same applies to paramilitaries. That's another category. And if they fall within the competence of the civilian judiciary, it was up to the civilian judiciary to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when would paramilitaries fall within the military jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for example, if they were part of the army and if while they were still in the army they had been arrested and so on and so forth. But from the point of time they left the army, the army could submit a criminal report but it would be the civilian judiciary that would deal with the cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, it may be a translation issue, but my understanding of the word "paramilitary" presupposes that the person is not in the military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, paramilitary or parapolice or whatever, but whoever puts on a uniform we call them paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: To continue on, to link up with what His Honour asked you. Please tell me, do you know what the Pauk or Spider group was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jugoslav Petrusic had a group. There were about 23 of them. They were in Kosovo. They were in Metohija, the border belt that is. They went there without going through the proper procedure and through the reception centre, although we do have information --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. What unit was that group a part of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Hypothetically speaking, had that group or members of that group committed crimes or criminal offences, who would have been competent to prosecute them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While they were still part of the army, had proceedings been instituted, it would have been done by the military judiciary. But from the moment they were sent back and dismissed from the army, then that case would have been handed over to the civilian judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But as long as they were members of the army they would fall within the competence, under the jurisdiction of the military courts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, have we finished with the 16th of May? Can we now deal with the 17th very briefly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't finished what I was saying. General Pavkovic said that this was one of the problems, and he proposed that a commission be established, that's the expression he used, which would have the task of establishing and drawing up a list, a correct list, which would show precisely what the army was suspected of, what the MUP was suspected of, and that commission would then set out to resolve all these problems. The whole process of investigation, gathering of evidence, and submitting criminal reports would be dealt with. He also spoke about the issue of volunteers. He said that as regards the volunteers joining the 3rd Army or the Pristina Corps, there were no serious problems. They were all going through the reception centre, but a certain number of them in the units had been causing trouble and those were sent back. He mentioned the example of the 175th Brigade, from which I believe 303 volunteers were sent back because of misbehaviour. That was what General Pavkovic said, that was the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And then on the 17th there was a meeting at President Milosevic's?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what happened at the meeting, it's already been mentioned elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all attended the meeting -- all of us who had attended the meeting on the 16th, that is. Milosevic chaired the meeting, and Mr. Sainovic and Rade Markovic, the chief of the state security sector, were also there. At the previous meeting of the 16th of May, it had been agreed after a brief introduction by Milosevic, General Vasiljevic should present his remarks followed by General Pavkovic. General Vasiljevic presented the information we had concerning the paramilitaries, he mentioned Boca, Jugoslav Petrusic, the Pauk group, the Drina Wolves, and Nedeljko Karisak, known as Legenda, and as far as I can remember he mentioned some operative groups and he said that there had been some problems and crimes connected with these. That was what he spoke about, and then he was followed by General Pavkovic, who repeated what he had said on the previous meeting, the meeting of the 16th of May, but he added a new proposal and this was that a state commission be set up to visit Kosovo and to help clarify all this. And his suggestion was supported by General Sainovic, who said it was a good idea. We left the meeting, however without this proposal being considered. We simply parted and that was it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 108, line 23, Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It said "General."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in paragraph 156 of your statement you described in detail the measures taken by the Army of Yugoslavia after the meeting in President Milosevic's office on the 17th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am not going to show this again. I simply ask you to refer to that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, a decision was made that a group should be sent to carry out an inspection and it would consist of you and General Vasiljevic, you would be members of the group. And a decision was made that this group should be sent to Kosovo urgently, that's in paragraph 157. Can you tell us what you learned and, first of all, when you visited Kosovo; and secondly, what you learned in relation to crimes that had been perpetrated.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything you've said is correct, but let me add something. I was not fully precise. After I signed the statement, I later realised that I had not been precise enough. General Ojdanic told us that we had to go to Kosovo, that's the real truth, but then a problem cropped up, the problem of an infantry brigade. It was the 7th Infantry Brigade. It was a brigade of reservists from the Krusevac area because a battalion had left its positions and arrived in Krusevac. And then the chief of the Supreme Command Staff said that General Vasiljevic and I should go to Krusevac to see what could be done about the situation and to send the battalion back. And we were engaged in that task until the 31st of May, which is why we were unable to go to Kosovo immediately. We completed that task on the 31st, and then we stayed in Kosovo from the 1st to the 7th. We visited 16 security organs, by means of briefings in the security section and later through visits to subordinate security organs, we didn't have time to go into every detail but the we gained an impression of the problem of war crimes and other activities contrary to the international laws of war. What we established was first that security organs were very active in investigating, documenting, and submitting criminal reports for the processing of these war crimes. But there was another problem. We in the security administration did not have information about this, so there was a problem in reporting. So we found that they were indeed very active, that they had the full support of the command, but that they did not submit reports on this. So that was the first time we heard about some of the crimes that had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, when you returned to Belgrade, did you submit a report and to whom?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We returned to Belgrade on the 7th and we immediately compiled a report consisting of two parts. There was a text and also tables, and 42 cases were dealt with in that report. There was some cases where more than one person was involved, for example, Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic and six others. General Farkas submitted the report to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command and he said that he would inform President Milosevic. This report went missing, and I know that General Ojdanic when preparing for this trial sought this document but was unable to find it. General Vasiljevic and I also searched for it but couldn't find it and I still fail to understand what happened to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please look at Defence Exhibit 3D479, that is a briefing of the 8th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 1, please. B/C/S page 2, please, line 4. Could we just lift up the B/C/S version a little bit. Thank you. And the text in English, we're interested in the last line of the first page and on page 2 -- in page 2, could we turn to page 2, please. Could you please turn to page 2 in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a briefing of the 8th of June and General Farkas's remarks. You did not attend that briefing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Farkas told me -- I was supposed to attend the briefing, but then he told me, I'll go, and what you and Aco found in Kosovo I will inform briefly the entire Supreme Command Staff about this. He probably spoke about this to the chief of the staff. I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you and General Farkas in the course of the war were not physically in the same buildings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were in the Supreme Command Staff and General Farkas was in another place where the security administration was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What General Farkas is saying here, these notes from the meeting, do they correspond to what you briefly told General Farkas at the meeting on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the core of the matter, that's the most important information that General Farkas felt had to be passed on to the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 4 in English and also page 4 in B/C/S, the bottom part of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, please look at the last two paragraphs of this text before you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of the Supreme Command Staff in the conclusions praised the security administration for the work they had done in Kosovo in connection with these problems, and he demanded that it should not stop at that, but that further action should be taken, that there should be documentation, investigation, and that investigation should be conducted against those who had committed crimes and other unlawful acts. And he even prioritized this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does this document refer to the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Judge Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was the report given to General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report was given I think already only the 8th, in the morning General Ojdanic had it. I'm not quite sure about the time. Possibly General Farkas took this with him when he went to the briefing. I cannot be very precise on that, but it had been completed by the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you didn't see it being handed over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that it was handed over on the 8th. Now, whether it was sent before the briefing or whether it was handed over on the 8th during the briefing on the 8th, whether it was handed over to General Ojdanic then, I cannot say. But we gave it to General Farkas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our last exhibit for today, 3D487.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, tell me what it is that you see before you now and explain it briefly, the first point, that is.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a meeting that was held, as far as I can remember, with military judicial organs, the Chief of General Staff on the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, look at the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the 8th of June. That is to say that meeting when General Farkas was there, when General Farkas was there. Then this had to do with the tasks that the Chief of Staff gave to the military judicial organs, and in relation to war crimes and other acts and contravention of international laws of war and cases that needed to be prosecuted, and then there are four numbers there. First are violations of international laws of war; second is crime; and then it's war crimes and so on and so forth; then desertion and other crimes. So he put in the first place what we had discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have less than half an hour left for this witness. If I organise myself even better, perhaps I'm going to cut it even shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want me to take a vote on what wants to stay and hear the next half-hour? I think Mr. Ackerman would be the first to volunteer. Before we decide on further action can I ask you one -- a question about one matter. You referred a number of times to the Supreme Command. What was the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Supreme Command was the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it from that answer it did not include the president of Serbia or the president of Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. They were the Supreme Defence Council which was a political body that made decisions from -- in the area of defence. The president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as Commander-in-Chief conveyed those decisions and issued orders to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, who further on through his own orders conveyed that to his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the Supreme Command always exist or did it come into existence at a particular time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I know - and I think that I do know - I think that from the point of view of the law things were not really regulated. There were proposals and some things were taken over from the former Yugoslavia when there was the Presidency as the collective organ. Some things were taken over but there wasn't enough time to define this in the constitution and in other laws.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the Supreme Defence Council meet in the months of March, April, May, and June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That completes our sitting for today, but you will require, I'm afraid, to return on Monday to continue with your evidence. The court will be sitting from 9.00 to 1.45 on Monday, so you should be here ready to resume your evidence at 9.00. It is extremely important, as I explained to you yesterday, that you don't discuss any aspect of the evidence in this case with anyone between now and Monday morning. Could you please now leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at 9.00 on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 10th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.35 p.m.,
